ops.old: The MassHealth ACO program offers three participation models: ACO-A (ACOs that partner with managed care organizations), ACO-B (ACOs that subcontract with existing MCOs for administrative services), and ACO-C (Primary Care Clinician ACOs for smaller practices). The program also features a PCMH+ model for patients with complex needs, providing enhanced care management payments and allowing greater flexibility in covered services.
ops.new: The MassHealth ACO program, which went live March 1, 2018 with 17 ACOs, offered three participation models: Accountable Care Partnership Plans (Model A — primary care networks exclusively partnered with a managed care organization and paid a prospective capitation rate, taking full insurance risk), Primary Care ACOs (Model B — contracting directly with MassHealth, paid fee-for-service and accountable for cost and quality but not insurance risk), and MCO-Administered ACOs (Model C — primary care networks contracting with one or more MCOs).
ops.claim: MassHealth ACO models described as ACO-A/B/C with a PCMH+ model
ops.sources: MassHealth All Provider Bulletin 272 (Nov 2017) and MassHealth ACO Models Q&A (mass.gov): Accountable Care Partnership Plans, Primary Care ACOs, MCO-Administered ACOs; 17 ACOs effective 2018-03-01. PCMH+ is Connecticut Medicaid's program, not MassHealth's
ops.note: Model definitions were wrong and PCMH+ was misattributed to Massachusetts.

ops.old: found that the program generated significant savings — an estimated $256 million over 4 years — with simultaneous quality improvements on multiple measures.
ops.new: found that over its first four years (2009–2012) the AQC reduced spending by 6.8% relative to a control group, with simultaneous quality improvements on multiple measures.
ops.claim: Song et al. NEJM: AQC saved an estimated $256 million over 4 years
ops.sources: Song Z, Rose S, Safran DG, Landon BE, Day MP, Chernew ME. Changes in health care spending and quality 4 years into global payment. N Engl J Med 2014;371:1704-14 (Commonwealth Fund summary: 6.8% lower spending vs control)
ops.note: $256M figure is not in the study; replaced with its headline result.

ops.old: Research consistently shows that clinical care accounts for only 20-30% of health outcomes, with the remainder driven by social factors including income, housing stability, food security, education, and social support networks.
ops.new: Widely used population-health models, such as the County Health Rankings model, attribute only about 20% of health outcomes to clinical care, with the remainder driven by health behaviors, social and economic factors such as income, housing stability, food security, education, and social support, and the physical environment.
ops.claim: Research consistently shows clinical care accounts for 20-30% of health outcomes
ops.sources: University of Wisconsin Population Health Institute, County Health Rankings model weights (clinical care 20%, health behaviors 30%, social and economic factors 40%, physical environment 10%)
ops.note: Range unsupported as stated; attributed to the model the figure actually comes from.
